items.title: New Home Sales Reinforce Last Month's Rebound
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>New home sales lost almost no ground in September, effectively reinforcing the healthy rebound seen in August's report.   The Census Bureau's New Residential Construction report clocked sales at an annual pace of 676k, down only 0.6% month over month. As seen in the chart below, the broader trend has been sideways for nearly 3 years now.    The number of new houses for sale slipped to  476,000 , down 1.0% from August and 2.3% from a year earlier. With inventory edging lower alongside sales, the implied supply eased to  8.4 months , compared with 8.5 months in August and 8.2 months last September.  Prices rebounded from August's decline. The median sales price rose to  $400,400 , up 3.9% for the month but still 3.9% below September 2025. The average sales price increased 0.4% to  $472,800 , leaving it 6.7% below its year-ago level. As a reminder, these figures are broadly based and don't factor in location, lot size, and other key pricing components

items.title: Home Price Appreciation Edges Higher in August
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content: <article>Home price appreciation picked up again in August (as reported this week), but the improvement was minimal.   The FHFA House Price Index rose  0.3%  from July to August, bringing annual appreciation to  2.4% . July's previously reported monthly gain was revised down from 0.3% to 0.2%. Regional results remained uneven, with annual appreciation ranging from 0.5% in the Mountain division to 4.4% in the East North Central division.  Case-Shiller's national index rose  2.1%  year over year, up from 1.9% in July. The 10-City Composite gained  3.6% , while the 20-City Composite rose  2.7% .    Even with the recent improvement, the inflation-adjusted trend remains negative. Consumer prices rose 3.4% annually in August, well above the 2.1% increase in national home prices. That gap has persisted for more than a year, offering some relief on a relative affordability basis even as elevated home prices and mortgage rates continue to challenge buyers.  Case-Shiller's metro-level results continued to show a sharp divide between markets. Chicago led the 20 tracked cities for the  sixth consecutive month , with prices up 6.7% year over year. New York followed at 6.2%, and Cleveland gained 4.3%. Seattle remained at the other end of the spectrum, with prices down  2.0%  annually, followed by Las Vegas at -1.3% and Denver at -0.8%.   FHFA House Price Index</article>

items.title: Mortgage Demand Bounces Back, Sort Of
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>Mortgage applications finally rebounded as mortgage rates fell for a second straight week. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  3.4% increase  in total application volume for the week ending October 23.  The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate declined to  7.37%  from 7.41%, its lowest level in three weeks. Both purchase and refinance applications moved higher, but just barely, and well below levels from last year.  The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index rose  4%  for the week, and still  18% below year-ago levels . Refinances increased 3%, offering only a modest rebound from a market still  61% below  its level a year earlier.      “The decline in rates gave borrowers some relief, with applications rebounding slightly, particularly conventional applications,” said MBA's Joel Kan. He noted that mortgage rates remain more than a percentage point above year-ago levels, while most homeowners have little incentive to refinance. Adjustable-rate mortgages accounted for  11.3% of applications , the highest share in more than a year, as borrowers sought lower monthly payments.   Mortgage Rate Summary:

items.title: Mortgage Applications Aren't Ready to Rebound Just Yet
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>Mortgage applications continued to decline even as mortgage rates finally moved lower. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  5.3% drop  in total application volume for the week ending October 16, despite the first weekly decline in mortgage rates in more than two months.  The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate fell to  7.41%  from 7.50% the previous week. That improvement wasn't enough to revive demand, with both purchase and refinance applications moving lower.  The seasonally adjusted Purchase Index fell  7%  for the week and was  18% below year-ago levels . Refinances fared somewhat better, declining 2%, though activity remained  59% lower  than a year earlier.  “Purchase applications fell 18 percent behind last year's pace, as higher rates are pricing buyers out of the market,” said MBA's Joel Kan, who also noted that adjustable-rate mortgages remain an option for qualified borrowers looking for lower rates. ARMs held steady at  10.5% of applications , with rates nearly a full percentage point below the 30-year fixed average.  The refinance share of total applications increased to  39.0%  from 37.7% the previous week. That shift came despite the decline in refinance volume, reflecting the steeper drop in purchase applications.   Mortgage Rate Summary:

items.title: Building Permits Hold Steady Despite Slide in Housing Starts
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content: <article>Residential construction failed to find even footing in September, with housing starts declining and single-family building permits pulling back, while total permits held nearly steady and completions edged higher. This week's Census Bureau data highlights weakness in new construction, particularly on the single-family side, while starts and completions were comparatively stable.    Privately owned housing starts fell  5.2%  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  1.221 million , down  7.4%  from September 2025. Single-family starts declined  4.6%  to  859k , and multi-family came in at  349k .  Building permits were more stable, slipping just  0.2%  to an annual rate of  1.400 million , although they were  3.0%  below the September 2025 pace. Single-family authorizations fell  4.0%  to  845k , while multi-family permits rose to  503k .  The contrast between total permits and single-family authorizations suggests that the overall pipeline for future construction was relatively steady, even as the single-family segment weakened. Multi-family permits accounted for a larger share of total authorizations in September, though monthly figures can fluctuate considerably in that segment.    Housing completions bounced back from last month, and increased  2.2%  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  1.192 million , still  14.0%  below the September 2025 rate. Single-family completions slipped  2.4%  to  840k , multi-family completions came in at  339k .</article>

items.title: Builder Confidence Hits Lowest Level Since 2012
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>The National Association of Home Builders (NAHB)/Wells Fargo Housing Market Index (HMI) dropped three points to  29  in October--its lowest level in 14 years. As per usual, higher mortgage rates, rising costs, and worsening labor and lot conditions were the driving factors.     All three component indices declined, with prospective buyer traffic suffering the steepest drop.

  "Buyer traffic has now fallen to its lowest level since April 2012, excluding the initial pandemic shock in April 2020.” said NAHB Chairman Bill Owens. Builders are also facing higher construction loan, material and diesel costs, along with construction delays tied to immigration enforcement activity.  Builders have responded by continuing to slash prices. The share reporting price cuts climbed to  43%  in October, the highest level during the 2020-2026 period. The average reduction remained at  6%  for the seventh consecutive month. Sales incentives were reported by 65% of builders, marking the 19th straight month that at least 60% have offered them.</article>

items.title: Existing Home Sales Treading Same Old Water
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content: <article>If you're busy, we can make this quick. Existing home sales dropped sharply from over 6m units per year starting in 2022 and had bottomed out around 4m units per year by the end of 2023. They've done essentially nothing exciting since then and the latest update is no exception. The end.     If you prefer to read an article-sized article, here you go:  Existing-home sales edged higher in September with The National Association of REALTORS® reporting a  1.5% increase  to a seasonally adjusted annual rate of  3.99 million . August and September mark the two slowest months for home sales this year, as higher borrowing costs continued to limit the pool of qualified buyers.  “Further increases in mortgage rates in recent weeks mean fewer buyers can qualify to purchase a home,” Yun said. Freddie Mac's average 30-year fixed rate climbed to  6.86% in September , up from 6.67% in August and 6.35% a year earlier.  Inventory continued to offer buyers more options than they had a year ago, although the latest increase was relatively modest. Total housing inventory reached  1.60 million units , up  1.9% from August  and  4.6% year over year .  Buyers may also have more room to negotiate as homes take longer to sell. The median time on market increased to  33 days , up from 31 days in August. Yun said the combination of higher inventory and longer selling times could require sellers to offer price reductions or other incentives to attract buyers.</article>

items.title: Only a Modest Decline For Mortgage Apps. Next Week Should Improve
items.author: Mortgage News Daily
items.content:
<article>Mortgage applications continued to lose ground as mortgage rates held near their highest levels in nearly three years. The Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) reported a  2.7% decline  in total mortgage application volume for the week ending October 9.  That's an important date, because a substantial majority of a fairly sharp decline in interest rates occurred AFTER October 9. As such, next week's data is a great opportunity to see the impact of lower rates.   Purchase activity took another step back, with the seasonally adjusted Purchase Index falling  4%  for the week and running  16% below year-ago levels . Refinances were nearly unchanged, slipping just 0.4%, but remained  56% lower  than a year earlier.  The average 30-year fixed mortgage rate edged up to  7.50% , its highest level since November 2023 and more than a percentage point above its level a year ago. MBA's Joel Kan notes,  “As a result, borrowers continue to rely more on ARM loans to help lower their monthly payments."   ARMs accounted for  10.5% of all applications , the highest share since October 2025. The refinance share also ticked higher, reaching 37.7% of total applications from 37.0% the previous week, with a 5% drop in FHA refinance applications being the main driver of the small overall decline.
